title: lab.common.page_archive wired into lab.common.working_memory as a disk-backed RAM cap on cross-page memory
goal: Bound lab.common.working_memory.WorkingMemory's own in-RAM page list, which grew by one digest per leaf for as long as a document was being written with no cap at all -- the project owner's own named concern that this would 'explode' on a long enough document -- the same way a person writing something long keeps a short active working set in mind and files everything older away as reference material, not held or re-read in full.
method: A direct WorkingMemory unit test (5 pages, ram_budget=2, the 5th page's claim deliberately conflicts with the 1st, long since evicted) checking the RAM cap holds, the archived-page contradiction is still caught, and dependency_tree still covers every page. Then the identical mechanism exercised through the real lab.common.brain.reason entry point (5 real entity leaves, working_memory_ram_budget=2 vs. the parameter omitted) checking the cap, the archive count, and that omitting the parameter leaves today's behavior completely unchanged.
results_prose: Direct unit test: 5 pages, ram_budget=2 -- RAM never holds more than 2 pages at once (['L3', 'L4']), 3 archived to disk. Page L4's claim conflicts with L0 (ram-evicted 3 pages earlier) -- correctly still caught: True. dependency_tree reports all 5 pages, archived or not. Through the real lab.common.brain.reason entry point, 5 entity leaves with working_memory_ram_budget=2: RAM capped at 2 pages, 3 archived, decision='supported'. With the parameter omitted entirely (today's existing behavior): RAM holds all 5 pages, zero archived, decision='supported' -- unaffected.
conclusion: lab.common.page_archive is now wired into lab.common.working_memory as working_memory_ram_budget= / working_memory_overflow_path= (both default None, zero regression for every existing caller), bounding the one place the controller's own cross-page memory grew without limit for the duration of a document-write call. The part a shallow cap would have gotten wrong is proven directly: a contradiction against a page that aged out of RAM onto disk many evictions ago is still caught, and that page still appears in the document's own provenance tree -- archiving a page changes WHERE it lives, never whether this project's own checks can still see it.
scale_down: 5 pages, ram_budget=2 -- a proof the cap, archive, and recall-from-disk cycle work correctly end to end and preserve provenance, not a capacity or performance benchmark for a genuinely long (hundreds/thousands-of-leaf) document.
follow_ups: Only WorkingMemory.pages (the controller's cross-page digest list) is bounded by this -- write_long_document's own `rendered_units` list (every leaf's full rendered text, held in RAM until joined into one `document_text` string at the end) is NOT touched here; that is a separate, larger architectural question (brain.reason's document_write branch returns that full text as the answer itself, so eliminating it would change what a caller gets back, not just how it's held internally) and was deliberately not forced into this scoped change.

page_archive's lookup is an exact (subject, verb_lemma) key match, the same access pattern lab.common.memory's notes table already uses -- it deliberately does not use lab.common.nested_index's hierarchical/semantic navigation, which answers a different question (what is this branch ABOUT) that cross-page consistency checking has never needed. If a future need arises to search archived pages by topic rather than by exact claim, that is a real, separate extension, not implied by this one.

No eviction policy beyond strict oldest-first exists (no 'pin this page' concept, unlike lab.common.paged.WorkingSet's relevance-based eviction for retrieval) -- for cross-page consistency checking specifically, recency is not actually the right signal (an old page is exactly as able to conflict with a new one as a recent page is), but the archive's exact-key lookup already makes that largely moot: an archived page is still fully checkable, just not held in RAM, so no page's claim is ever truly lost regardless of eviction order.
models_used: None -- page_archive is deterministic SQLite with an index on (subject, verb_lemma); no model of any kind is involved in archiving or recall.
